Computer Science Labs

Image Processing · Lab 10 · Material

Dataset Quality and Splits

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Turn a folder-like collection into a dataset whose contents and boundaries you can explain. Audit the images, preserve review decisions and keep related views together before later preprocessing or augmentation.

What you will learn

  • Record decode failures, source modes and realized output geometry.
  • Distinguish identical files, identical decoded pixels and uncertain near-duplicate candidates.
  • Use quality measurements as review flags with stated limitations.
  • Build and audit object-group splits with class counts and reproducible provenance.

Before this lab: Complete Labs 01–09 and understand decoding, image geometry, filtering and normalization contracts.

In this lab

  1. Decode inventories and quarantine records
  2. Canonical representations and conversion records
  3. File identity and decoded-pixel identity
  4. Near-duplicate candidates and uncertainty
  5. Quality flags and their limits
  6. Object-group splits
  7. Leakage audits beyond filenames
  8. Class counts and reproducible provenance

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Run once. records contains 24 original 160-by-128 drawings: two views of each of six books and six mugs. payloads adds varied encoded inputs and one deliberate decode failure.

Python · shared setup
import io
import hashlib
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageOps, UnidentifiedImageError
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(210)

# Original drawings represent two existing views of each of twelve household objects.
# Object groups, not individual views, are the independent units in this toy collection.
def draw_object(kind,index,view):
    height,width = 128,160
    yy,xx = np.mgrid[:height,:width]
    generator = np.random.default_rng(410+index+(100 if kind=="mug" else 0))
    grain = generator.normal(0,1.1,(height,width))+4*np.sin(yy*0.6)
    base = 174+18*xx/(width-1)+grain
    background = np.stack([base+16,base,base-22],axis=-1)
    image = Image.fromarray(np.clip(np.rint(background),0,255).astype(np.uint8))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(image)
    dx,dy = 3*view,-2*view
    if kind=="book":
        palette = [(166,50,58),(48,85,166),(58,116,77),(128,65,133),(151,100,35),(50,116,127)]
        color = palette[index-1]
        draw.rectangle((34+dx,13+dy,111+dx,110+dy),fill=color,outline=(35,37,43),width=2)
        draw.rectangle((35+dx,15+dy,44+dx,108+dy),fill=(46,44,48))
        draw.rectangle((52+dx,28+dy,100+dx,53+dy),fill=(240,231,205))
        draw.text((57+dx,34+dy),"NOTES",fill=(43,44,51))
        for y in range(91,107,3):
            draw.line((47+dx,y+dy,108+dx,y+dy),fill=(228,223,202),width=1)
    else:
        palette = [(232,229,210),(149,197,202),(230,188,136),(185,178,219),(194,214,162),(223,164,168)]
        color = palette[index-1]
        draw.ellipse((105+dx,49+dy,141+dx,91+dy),outline=color,width=8)
        draw.rounded_rectangle((45+dx,36+dy,112+dx,110+dy),radius=12,fill=color,outline=(86,89,91),width=2)
        draw.ellipse((45+dx,25+dy,112+dx,49+dy),fill=(240,235,216),outline=(79,77,65),width=2)
        draw.ellipse((51+dx,30+dy,106+dx,43+dy),fill=(86,49,28))
        draw.text((66+dx,66+dy),"TEA",fill=(50,79,93))
        draw.line((53+dx,49+dy,53+dx,95+dy),fill=(248,246,228),width=2)
    draw.rectangle((5,115,72,125),fill=(230,220,180))
    draw.text((9,115),f"item {index}",fill=(50,47,36))
    return np.asarray(image).copy()

records = []
for kind in ("book","mug"):
    for index in range(1,7):
        group = f"{kind}{index:02}"
        for view in (0,1):
            records.append({"id":f"{group}-v{view+1}","group":group,"label":kind,"image":draw_object(kind,index,view)})
rgb = records[0]["image"].copy()
h,w = rgb.shape[:2]
# Varied source modes/sizes for the audit exercises; no external image files are used.
rgba_source = Image.fromarray(rgb).convert("RGBA")
rgba_source.putalpha(190)
mode_sources = [
    Image.fromarray(rgb),
    Image.fromarray(rgb).convert("L"),
    rgba_source,
    Image.fromarray(cv2.resize(rgb,(120,96),interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA))
]
payloads = {}
for name,image in zip(["book.png","gray.png","alpha.png","small.png"],mode_sources):
    stream = io.BytesIO()
    image.save(stream,format="PNG")
    payloads[name] = stream.getvalue()
payloads["broken.png"] = b"not an encoded image"

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Decode inventories and quarantine records

Dataset preparation begins with an inventory, not with a training array. A filename or extension does not prove that its bytes contain a usable image. Pillow can open a header before decoding all pixels, so call load inside the error-handling boundary. Record the source mode and dimensions only after successful decoding, and keep failures attached to their original IDs.

Audit the five in-memory payloads from setup. Four are valid PNGs with deliberately different modes or sizes; one is a short invalid byte string. The error record remains visible in the report rather than being silently skipped or replaced by a black image. Replacing a failure with plausible pixels would turn a technical problem into misleading data. This audit does not decide whether a successfully decoded image is appropriate for the intended task. It separates a definite read failure from later questions about colour evidence, size, quality or labels. For external collections, also impose sensible file and dimension limits and retain the decoder's normal safeguards. The tiny fixtures here keep the example focused on complete decoding and traceable outcomes.

Try it

  1. Decode every payload fully inside a narrow exception boundary.
  2. Keep success metadata and failure reasons by source ID.
  3. Display successful examples beside an explicit failure panel.
Python · run in order
audit = []
decoded = {}
for name,payload in payloads.items():
    try:
        with Image.open(io.BytesIO(payload)) as opened:
            opened.load()
            decoded[name] = opened.copy()
            audit.append({"id":name,"status":"decoded","mode":opened.mode,"size":opened.size})
    except (UnidentifiedImageError,OSError) as error:
        audit.append({"id":name,"status":"quarantine","reason":type(error).__name__})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,5,figsize=(15,3.2))
for ax,row in zip(axes,audit):
    if row["status"]=="decoded":
        ax.imshow(decoded[row["id"]],cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=255)
        ax.set_title(f'{row["id"]}\n{row["mode"]}, {row["size"]}',fontsize=9)
    else:
        ax.text(0.5,0.5,"Decode failed\nkept in audit",ha="center",va="center",transform=ax.transAxes)
        ax.set_title(row["id"],fontsize=9)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print(audit)

Read the result

The gray, alpha-bearing and small images decoded successfully but still need an explicit input policy. The broken payload has a record and a reason, with no invented substitute image.

Change and compare

  • Append an exact copy of one valid payload under a new ID and inspect the audit size.
  • Compare a header-only open with full load when reasoning about truncated files.

Guided task 02

Canonical representations and conversion records

A common array shape makes batching convenient, but it should not hide how each source was interpreted. Our audit policy first applies EXIF orientation, then composites any transparency onto white, converts to RGB and fits the result inside a 160-by-128 canvas. The remaining canvas also uses white. Record the original mode and dimensions alongside the actual resized dimensions and padding offsets.

This policy accepts grayscale input by repeating its available intensity information into RGB. It does not reconstruct the missing colours. Compositing transparency also depends on the chosen background and is not a reversible mode change. The fixture with smaller dimensions is enlarged under a declared linear interpolation policy; shrinking would use area interpolation. All of these choices can matter to a later task even when every result ends with identical dtype and shape. Keep source files and source metadata so reviewers can distinguish original evidence from processing choices. Canonicalization here is deterministic and contains no learned dataset statistic. Its rules should be fixed before evaluation, and any later training-only random variants should inherit their source group rather than entering the split as independent images.

Try it

  1. Orient, composite and convert each valid source under one explicit policy.
  2. Fit its RGB pixels to a common canvas.
  3. Record source and realized geometry for each result.
Python · run in order
canonical = []
conversion_records = []
for source in mode_sources:
    oriented = ImageOps.exif_transpose(source)
    rgba = oriented.convert("RGBA")
    flattened = Image.alpha_composite(Image.new("RGBA",rgba.size,(255,255,255,255)),rgba).convert("RGB")
    array = np.asarray(flattened)
    source_h,source_w = array.shape[:2]
    ratio = min(160/source_w,128/source_h)
    new_w,new_h = round(source_w*ratio),round(source_h*ratio)
    method = cv2.INTER_AREA if ratio<1 else cv2.INTER_LINEAR
    resized = cv2.resize(array,(new_w,new_h),interpolation=method)
    left,top = (160-new_w)//2,(128-new_h)//2
    output = np.full((128,160,3),255,dtype=np.uint8)
    output[top:top+new_h,left:left+new_w] = resized
    canonical.append(output)
    conversion_records.append({"source_mode":source.mode,"source_size":source.size,"oriented_size":oriented.size,"resized_size":(new_w,new_h),"offset":(left,top),"scale":(new_w/source_w,new_h/source_h)})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,4,figsize=(12,5.5))
for index,(source,result) in enumerate(zip(mode_sources,canonical)):
    axes[0,index].imshow(source,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=255)
    axes[0,index].set_title(f"Input {source.mode}, {source.size}",fontsize=9)
    axes[1,index].imshow(result)
    axes[1,index].set_title("RGB uint8, 160 x 128",fontsize=9)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The common output contract hides differences unless the conversion record travels with it. A grayscale source remains missing colour evidence, and the alpha-bearing source has been flattened onto the stated background.

Change and compare

  • Choose a dark compositing background and identify which source changes.
  • Replace one source with a tall image and inspect the actual padding offsets.

Guided task 03

File identity and decoded-pixel identity

An exact file hash describes the encoded bytes, including compression choices and metadata. Two files can contain the same decoded picture while having different byte hashes. Conversely, a checksum does not describe whether two differently sampled or compressed pictures show the same physical object. Choose the identity question before choosing a fingerprint.

Encode the same RGB drawing as PNG with two compression settings and as JPEG. Compare file-byte SHA-256 digests, then decode the files and fingerprint a declared RGB representation. The pixel fingerprint includes shape, dtype, channel-order tag and row-major pixel bytes so that interpretation is part of the record. The two PNG encodings retain the same decoded samples but differ as files. JPEG may change samples even when it still shows the same book. Matching digests are useful for finding candidate exact groups; verify pixel equality within such a group before making a consequential deletion decision. Retain source IDs and labels while investigating duplicates, because an exact image carrying conflicting labels is a metadata problem rather than a reason to discard an arbitrary row without review.

Try it

  1. Encode two PNG versions and a JPEG from the same pixels.
  2. Compute file and decoded-representation fingerprints separately.
  3. Compare decoded arrays and a JPEG difference image.
Python · run in order
encoded = {}
for name,format_name,settings in [("png0","PNG",{"compress_level":0}),("png9","PNG",{"compress_level":9}),("jpeg","JPEG",{"quality":70})]:
    stream = io.BytesIO()
    Image.fromarray(rgb).save(stream,format=format_name,**settings)
    encoded[name] = stream.getvalue()
file_hashes = {name:hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest() for name,payload in encoded.items()}
decoded_rgb = {}
for name,payload in encoded.items():
    with Image.open(io.BytesIO(payload)) as source:
        source.load()
        decoded_rgb[name] = np.array(source.convert("RGB"))
def pixel_digest(array):
    header = f"RGB|{array.shape}|{array.dtype.str}|".encode("ascii")
    return hashlib.sha256(header+array.tobytes(order="C")).hexdigest()
pixel_hashes = {name:pixel_digest(array) for name,array in decoded_rgb.items()}
jpeg_error = np.max(np.abs(decoded_rgb["jpeg"].astype(np.int16)-rgb.astype(np.int16)),axis=2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(12,3.2))
for ax,name in zip(axes[:3],["png0","png9","jpeg"]):
    ax.imshow(decoded_rgb[name])
    ax.set_title(name)
error_image = axes[3].imshow(jpeg_error,cmap="magma",vmin=0,vmax=max(1,int(jpeg_error.max())))
axes[3].set_title("JPEG channel error")
fig.colorbar(error_image, ax=axes[3], label="Maximum absolute channel difference", shrink=0.75)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("File:",file_hashes,"Pixels:",pixel_hashes)

Read the result

The PNG pair shares decoded-pixel identity without sharing file-byte identity. The JPEG remains a related view of the same synthetic object even though exact pixel matching can fail.

Change and compare

  • Compare an exact byte copy under a new source ID.
  • Explain why a pixel fingerprint must include the array shape and representation convention.

Guided task 04

Near-duplicate candidates and uncertainty

An exact match is too strict for related images that differ in compression, small camera movement or appearance. A simple similarity descriptor can help prioritize review, but it cannot prove that two images are the same object. Here a descriptor is a 16-by-16 grayscale thumbnail in unit range. Its mean absolute difference gives one easily inspected distance, while deliberately discarding colour and fine detail.

Compare the first book with its second view, another physical book and a mug. Mark a pair as a review candidate when this illustrative distance is at most 0.10. The threshold is an exercise setting, not a validated duplicate detector. Similar backgrounds and object shapes can make distinct objects close under this descriptor, while a shift can move a true related pair farther apart. Keep every record and show the candidate flag alongside the images. Do not automatically merge groups or delete uncertain samples. Resolve trustworthy grouping information before the split, and log why any records are linked. A real collection would need candidate inspection suited to its sources and intended independence unit, such as object, capture session or person.

Try it

  1. Create normalized 16-square grayscale descriptors.
  2. Measure each comparison against the first book.
  3. Display candidate flags while retaining all source records.
Python · run in order
comparison_records = [records[0],records[1],records[2],records[12]]
def descriptor(image):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(image,cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
    return cv2.resize(gray,(16,16),interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)/255.0
reference_descriptor = descriptor(comparison_records[0]["image"])
distances = np.array([np.mean(np.abs(descriptor(r["image"])-reference_descriptor)) for r in comparison_records])
candidates = distances<=0.10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(12,3.3))
for ax,row,distance,candidate in zip(axes,comparison_records,distances,candidates):
    ax.imshow(row["image"])
    ax.set_title(f'{row["id"]}\ndistance {distance:.3f}; review {bool(candidate)}',fontsize=9)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

A low descriptor distance is a reason to inspect a pair, not permission to erase it. Compare the object-group IDs as well as appearance and notice information that the small grayscale descriptor cannot retain.

Change and compare

  • Compare descriptors using a larger thumbnail and inspect changed rankings.
  • Find two differently coloured inputs that become similar after grayscale conversion.

Guided task 05

Quality flags and their limits

Some problems require review even when decoding succeeds. Mean intensity can flag a very dark example, intensity standard deviation can flag a nearly constant image, and variance of a signed Laplacian response can flag a weak edge response. These are measurable properties, not universal quality scores. A smooth mug surface or a legitimately dark object can produce values that would be suspicious in a text-rich label image.

Create four controlled inputs: the original book, a darkened copy, a blurred copy and a constant field. Flag mean below 50, grayscale standard deviation below 8 and Laplacian variance below 25. These strict thresholds use byte-scale grayscale values and are illustrative review rules for this exercise. Their results depend on resolution, scene texture, conversion and filtering details; do not move them unchanged into every collection. Keep the actual measurements and reasons, then inspect the examples. The flat field is technically readable but lacks the expected scene content. Other flags can represent either a problem or a valid difficult example. Automatically discarding every flagged sample could remove important conditions that a later system needs to handle.

Try it

  1. Construct clearly labelled dark, blurred and constant diagnostic examples.
  2. Measure three defined grayscale properties.
  3. Attach review flags without deleting any image.
Python · run in order
quality_images = {
    "original":rgb,
    "dark":np.rint(rgb.astype(np.float32)*0.2).astype(np.uint8),
    "blurred":cv2.GaussianBlur(rgb,(13,13),3),
    "constant":np.full_like(rgb,128)
}
def quality_record(image):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(image,cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
    mean = float(gray.mean())
    spread = float(gray.std())
    edge_variance = float(cv2.Laplacian(gray,cv2.CV_64F).var())
    flags = []
    if mean<50:
        flags.append("dark")
    if spread<8:
        flags.append("low contrast")
    if edge_variance<25:
        flags.append("weak edge response")
    return {"mean":mean,"spread":spread,"edge_variance":edge_variance,"flags":flags}
quality = {name:quality_record(image) for name,image in quality_images.items()}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(13,3.7))
for ax,(name,image) in zip(axes,quality_images.items()):
    row = quality[name]
    ax.imshow(image)
    flags_text = ", ".join(row["flags"]) or "no flags"
    ax.set_title(f'{name}\nmean {row["mean"]:.1f}; std {row["spread"]:.1f}\nedge var {row["edge_variance"]:.1f}\n{flags_text}',fontsize=8)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Inspect the cause of each flag in its image. A number below a threshold is evidence about the stated measurement, not a general verdict about the label or usefulness of the record.

Change and compare

  • Change the output resolution before measuring edge variance and inspect its dependence on scale.
  • Describe a valid household scene that might have low contrast without being a corrupted file.

Guided task 06

Object-group splits

The independent unit in this collection is a household object, not an image row. Each book and mug has two existing synthetic views. If one view enters training and another enters evaluation, the two partitions share object-specific evidence even though their pixels are not identical. Assign a split to each object group first and let all of its rows inherit that decision.

Our deliberately small balanced policy allocates four groups of each class to training, one to validation and one to test. Shuffle the sorted group IDs with a local seed of 210 to make the assignment reproducible. The helper rejects duplicate record IDs, conflicting labels within a group and inputs that do not match this six-groups-per-class teaching policy. It is not a general guarantee of representativeness. More diverse real collections may need grouping by capture session, person or location, and rare classes can make desired allocations impossible. Establish trustworthy groups before creating any later random variants or fitting normalization statistics. Training variants stay with their source group; validation and test receive their fixed deterministic processing policies. A balanced count is only one audit, not proof that evaluation is independent or sufficiently broad.

Try it

  1. Validate object-group metadata.
  2. Assign six groups per class using the explicit 4/1/1 policy.
  3. Show representative views and confirm each group stays in one split.
Python · run in order
def assign_groups(rows,seed):
    if not rows or len({r["id"] for r in rows})!=len(rows):
        raise ValueError("Require nonempty records with unique IDs")
    group_labels = {}
    for row in rows:
        group,label = row["group"],row["label"]
        if label not in ("book","mug"):
            raise ValueError("Unexpected class")
        if group in group_labels and group_labels[group]!=label:
            raise ValueError("One object group has conflicting labels")
        group_labels[group] = label
    generator = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    assignment = {}
    for label in ("book","mug"):
        groups = sorted(g for g,value in group_labels.items() if value==label)
        if len(groups)!=6:
            raise ValueError("This teaching policy requires six groups per class")
        ordered = generator.permutation(groups)
        for group,split in zip(ordered,["train"]*4+["validation","test"]):
            assignment[str(group)] = split
    return assignment

split_by_group = assign_groups(records,210)
record_splits = {row["id"]:split_by_group[row["group"]] for row in records}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,3,figsize=(10,5.4))
for column,split in enumerate(["train","validation","test"]):
    for row_index,label in enumerate(["book","mug"]):
        example = next(r for r in records if r["label"]==label and record_splits[r["id"]]==split)
        axes[row_index,column].imshow(example["image"])
        axes[row_index,column].set_title(f'{split}: {example["group"]}',fontsize=10)
        axes[row_index,column].axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Group assignment:",split_by_group)

Read the result

Each displayed object belongs to one partition, and its undisplayed second view inherits that same assignment. The small class-balanced demonstration does not establish coverage of every real household condition.

Change and compare

  • Replay the policy with the same seed and compare the full assignment dictionary.
  • List which independence unit would be appropriate for images of the same room captured on one day.

Guided task 07

Leakage audits beyond filenames

A split can look sensible by row count while still sharing evidence across partitions. Group IDs catch related views when metadata is correct. Pixel fingerprints can expose an exact copy whose group metadata is missing or wrong. These checks complement each other: an exact pixel audit will miss many shifted or compressed views, and a group audit will miss a duplicate assigned an unrelated group name.

Build a deliberately faulty partition from a fixed group allocation. Move the second view of book01 into validation while its first view remains in training. Also add an exact copy of the first view to test under an unresolved group name. Audit both group-to-split sets and decoded-pixel-fingerprint-to-split sets, retaining the source IDs in each result. The point is to find the evidence-sharing problem before evaluation, not to obtain a larger-looking dataset by counting copies. Correct the grouping or split assignment with a recorded decision; do not silently discard whichever row happens to be encountered last. Re-run the full audit after any repair, because resolving one pair can connect a larger set of related records that must remain together.

Try it

  1. Construct two explicitly labelled metadata mistakes without changing the source records.
  2. Find groups and exact pixel candidates appearing in multiple splits.
  3. Display the implicated views and retain their identities for review.
Python · run in order
base_assignment = {r["id"]:("train" if int(r["group"][-2:])<=4 else "validation" if r["group"].endswith("05") else "test") for r in records}
faulty_assignment = base_assignment.copy()
faulty_assignment["book01-v2"] = "validation"
extra = {"id":"unresolved-copy","group":"unresolved","label":"book","image":records[0]["image"].copy()}
faulty_records = records+[extra]
faulty_assignment[extra["id"]] = "test"
group_partitions = {}
fingerprint_partitions = {}
fingerprint_ids = {}
for row in faulty_records:
    split = faulty_assignment[row["id"]]
    group_partitions.setdefault(row["group"],set()).add(split)
    array = row["image"]
    header = f"RGB|{array.shape}|{array.dtype.str}|".encode("ascii")
    digest = hashlib.sha256(header+array.tobytes(order="C")).hexdigest()
    fingerprint_partitions.setdefault(digest,set()).add(split)
    fingerprint_ids.setdefault(digest,[]).append(row["id"])
leaked_groups = {group for group,parts in group_partitions.items() if len(parts)>1}
exact_cross_split = [fingerprint_ids[digest] for digest,parts in fingerprint_partitions.items() if len(parts)>1]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(10,3.5))
for ax,row in zip(axes,[records[0],records[1],extra]):
    ax.imshow(row["image"])
    ax.set_title(f'{row["id"]}\n{faulty_assignment[row["id"]]} / group {row["group"]}',fontsize=9)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Group leakage:",leaked_groups,"Exact pixel candidates:",exact_cross_split)

Read the result

The related-view mistake is visible through the shared group ID. The exact-copy mistake remains detectable despite its different group name, and pixel equality can confirm that candidate.

Change and compare

  • Verify exact array equality for the copy pair before deciding how to repair its metadata.
  • Explain why a renamed, recompressed JPEG copy might require more than either of these exact checks.

Guided task 08

Class counts and reproducible provenance

A useful handoff records both image counts and independent-group counts. Sixteen training images in this fixture represent eight objects, not sixteen independent objects. Class balance measured by image rows can also conceal unequal numbers of views per group. Report both quantities for each partition, and inspect representative images alongside the numbers.

Recreate the seeded group assignment and build a manifest containing stable source ID, object group, label, split, array contract and a decoded-pixel fingerprint. Record the policy's seed, independence unit and per-class group allocation separately. This record makes the preparation route inspectable without claiming that a seed alone describes every processing choice. Hashes belong to a stated representation, and the manifest should be regenerated when pixels or grouping decisions change. The lesson leaves all fixtures in memory; a later project can serialize the reviewed record and processing configuration. No model is trained here, and the counts do not estimate future accuracy. Before a future handoff, resolve remaining decode or identity issues, fit learned statistics only on the training partition and keep evaluation preprocessing deterministic. A complete record supports those checks rather than replacing them.

Try it

  1. Rebuild the documented seeded group assignment.
  2. Create per-record provenance and per-split class counts.
  3. Compare image counts with independent-group counts.
Python · run in order
# Reuse the validated group-assignment rule from task 6.
split_by_group = assign_groups(records,210)
policy = {"seed":210,"independence_unit":"object_group","groups_per_class":{"train":4,"validation":1,"test":1},"source":"original synthetic RGB drawings"}
manifest = []
for row in records:
    array = row["image"]
    header = f"RGB|{array.shape}|{array.dtype.str}|".encode("ascii")
    manifest.append({"id":row["id"],"group":row["group"],"label":row["label"],"split":split_by_group[row["group"]],"shape":array.shape,"dtype":str(array.dtype),"channel_order":"RGB","pixel_sha256":hashlib.sha256(header+array.tobytes(order="C")).hexdigest()})
split_names = ["train","validation","test"]
class_names = ["book","mug"]
image_counts = np.array([[sum(r["split"]==split and r["label"]==label for r in manifest) for label in class_names] for split in split_names])
group_counts = np.array([[len({r["group"] for r in manifest if r["split"]==split and r["label"]==label}) for label in class_names] for split in split_names])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,3,figsize=(10,6))
positions = np.arange(2)
for column,split in enumerate(split_names):
    example = next(r for r in records if split_by_group[r["group"]]==split)
    axes[0,column].imshow(example["image"])
    axes[0,column].set_title(f'{split}: {example["id"]}',fontsize=10)
    axes[0,column].axis("off")
    axes[1,column].bar(positions-0.18,image_counts[column],width=0.36,label="images")
    axes[1,column].bar(positions+0.18,group_counts[column],width=0.36,label="groups")
    axes[1,column].set_xticks(positions,class_names)
    axes[1,column].set_ylim(0,9)
    axes[1,column].set_ylabel("Count")
    axes[1,column].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
print(policy)

Read the result

The image and group counts answer different questions about the same partition. A representative drawing helps keep the report connected to its contents, but it is not a substitute for auditing every record.

Change and compare

  • Give one object an extra existing view and compare the two count tables before splitting again.
  • List which manifest fields must change if the RGB conversion or object grouping is revised.
